name: Maxilla expansion for forward growth (face pulling/reverse-pull headgear)

lead: Reverse-pull headgear is an orthodontic device used in children with underbites and a recessed upper jaw to pull the maxilla forward.
Studies in children report forward skeletal change, though some patients relapse in the long term.

paras: Elastics from the teeth to a frame on the forehead and chin apply forward force, often after rapid palatal expansion, to remodel the sutures around the maxilla.
Dentoalveolar side effects and relapse are reported. Use is guided by an orthodontist, and the evidence concerns growing children.

lead: Reverse-pull headgear, also called a facemask or protraction facemask, is an orthodontic appliance with a frame in front of the face resting on the forehead and chin, with elastics attached to the teeth to pull the upper jaw forward.[1] It is used in children with Class III malocclusion and a retrusive maxilla, often together with rapid palatal expansion.[2]

Orthodontic literature reports that treatment in the deciduous and mixed dentition can produce skeletal forward movement of the maxilla through remodeling of the circummaxillary sutures,[2][3] though it is often accompanied by dentoalveolar effects.[4] Long-term follow-up shows that some patients relapse.[5]
In appearance communities the entry is discussed as a way to move the midface forward, and the evidence concerns growing children, not adults.
infobox: About 14 to 16 hours daily, per Wikipedia[1]

paras: A facemask pulls forward and downward on the upper jaw, the opposite direction of conventional headgear.[1] It is paired with rapid palatal expansion in many protocols, which is thought to loosen the sutures.[2]

The literature has recommended starting before age 8, though one study stated that this had not been supported by scientific data and examined patients younger and older than 8.[2] Another study of 60 Japanese children in mixed dentition examined whether bone age helps plan treatment timing.[3]

A cephalometric study of 41 Class III children found that outcomes were assessed at 5 and, for 18 patients, 10 years after treatment, grouping patients into success or failure; the study explored predictors of long-term failure.[5] A clinical trial in Chinese adolescents examined the effects of maxillary protraction and long-term stability.[6] A Cochrane-style trial cited on Wikipedia suggests early facemask treatment may reduce later need for orthognathic surgery.[1]

Case series with intermaxillary elastics anchored to miniplates in children aged 10 to 13 aimed to achieve skeletal changes with fewer unwanted dentoalveolar effects.[4] Ex-vivo work has studied sutural deformation during bone-anchored protraction.[7]

Clinical studies exist in children with Class III malocclusion: cephalometric follow-ups, a clinical trial in adolescents and small case series.[4][5][6] No studies on adults using facemasks for appearance were found.
